title: On average, satellite-mapped wildfire smoke did not decrease butterfly, bee or dragonfly shares of iNaturalist records, or total records, in 274 US two-degree boxes in April-September 2017-2025
abstract: Question: Does wildfire smoke decrease iNaturalist records of sun-dependent insects (butterflies, bees, dragonflies and damselflies) relative to other organisms, and does it decrease total recording effort? Data: 98.9 million verifiable iNaturalist records in 274 two-degree boxes over the contiguous US (April-September 2017-2025; 450,928 box-days), NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons (box area fractions by density class) and NASA POWER daily weather. Method: binomial logit of the focal share relative to a same-day reference group (plants, all other records, or moths), with box-year-month fixed effects, day-of-week and weather controls (equal to stacked Poisson with box-day fixed effects); placebo smoke 7 days before and after; four region-period samples; fungi and birds as controls; Poisson effort models; a solar-radiation benchmark. Results: full medium-or-heavy cover changed the butterfly share by +0.5% (95% CI -2.1 to +3.1) relative to plants and -0.9% (-4.0 to +2.2) relative to moths; Odonata -1.4% (-4.8 to +2.1); bees +3.1% (+0.2 to +5.9). Placebo days gave similar values. Heavy smoke increased the bee share by 9% (5 to 13), but this came mainly from the 2023 eastern smoke and was +3.0% (-1.7 to +7.8) without 2023. Total records changed by +1.3% (-0.4 to +3.0). Heavy smoke lowered cloud-adjusted all-sky radiation by 1.69 MJ/m2/day; this light loss predicts a 5% butterfly decrease, above the observed +1.2% (-3.4 to +5.8). Fungi decreased under smoke, which shows a dryness confound. Limitations: 18 of 56 region-period estimates excluded zero with both signs, so the CIs are too narrow and single-region effects up to about 10% are possible; 2-degree, whole-day exposure; column smoke, not surface PM2.5; records mix activity, detectability and observer choice. Conclusion: same-day smoke is not a large or consistent bias in iNaturalist insect records at this scale.

citations.reason: Smoke vs Breeding Bird Survey test; we reuse the HMS retrieval recipe and placebo design and extend the question to insects and unstructured citizen-science effort.
Earlier campaign evidence that smoke changes the light environment (PhenoCam colour fractions).
HMS medium-or-heavy smoke captures only part of elevated surface PM2.5 dates; this limits our exposure measure.
Systematic review of landscape fire smoke and insects; little field evidence on insect flight under smoke.
eBird study of PM2.5 effects on bird detection (Sanderfoot and Gardner 2021).
